terms.comment: The ordinary word in comedy and prose, literally “she who earns”.

terms.gloss: be a prostitute (literally: stand out for sale)

terms.comment: The participle of prōstituō, used as a noun; not entered as a noun in Lewis & Short.

evidence: Plaut. Am. 1.1.132; Ter. Eun. 3.1.34; Cic. Mil. 21.55 (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally a hide; a coarser, contemptuous word than meretrīx, used of male prostitutes too (Cic. Phil. 2.44, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Ep. 3.3.22; Cic. Mil. 21.55; Liv. 1.4.7 (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The slang that gives lupānar, a brothel.

evidence: Plaut. Aul. 285: Bellum et pudīcum vērō prōstibulum poplī.
Plaut. Cist. 331: nam meretrīcem astāre in viā sōlam prōstibulī sānest
terms.comment: From prōstāre, to stand out in front for hire. The line of the Cistellaria sets her below the meretrīx: standing alone in the street is what a prōstibulum does.

terms.gloss: earn one’s living with one’s body: work as a prostitute
evidence: Plaut. Poen. 1140: facerentque indignum genere quaestum corpore
terms.comment: The plain phrase of prose (Livy, Tacitus). Also without corpore: quaestum occipit, she takes up the trade (Ter. And. 79).

phrases.latin: nam meretrīcem astāre in viā sōlam prōstibulī sānest
phrases.english: for a courtesan to stand alone in the street is surely the mark of a common prostitute
